headline: The merchant's しょうにん is Chinese; the native word looks like “trade-person”, あきびと.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 商人 (MC syang nyin).

headline: “So to speak” is a “say” in a hypothetical form: “if one were to say”.

sources.quote: The Classical Japanese conditional form of the verb 言う (iu, “to say, to speak”): 言わ (iwa, 未然形 (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) of the verb 言う (iu)) + ば (-ba, an inflectional suffix indicating the hypothetical condition).

headline: Salad is an internationalism — Wiktionary lists English, French and Portuguese as candidate sources.

sources.quote: Internationalism of uncertain specifics, variously proposed to derive from English salad, French salade or Portuguese salada.

headline: Politely “your daughter” puts an honorific on both sides of a word for an “unmarried woman”.

sources.quote: Of お (honorific prefix) + 嬢 (jō, “unmarried woman; daughter”) + さん (honorific suffix)

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
headline: Work is “doing” plus “thing”, and the 仕 is only ateji.

sources.quote: From し (shi, “doing”, continuative form of する (suru, “to do”)) + 事 (koto, “thing; stuff”). The koto reading for 事 changes to goto as an instance of rendaku (連濁). 仕 is ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

headline: Here the same character is read twice, once the native way and once the Chinese way.

sources.quote: Compound of 日(ひ) (hi, “sun; day”, using the native Japanese reading) + 日(にち) (nichi, “sun; day”, using the Chinese-derived reading).

headline: Monday is “moon day”, a name that came from Chinese astrology in the Heian period.

sources.quote: /getueubi/ > /getuyoːbi/.
Compound of 月曜 (getsuyō, “moon”, in reference also to the day for that celestial body, as originally imported from Chinese astrology in the Heian period) + 日 (hi, “day”).

The compound form suffixed with 日 (hi, “day”) appears in common use from the Meiji period with the promulgation of the Gregorian calendar. See also Names of the days of the week on Wikipedia.Wikipedia

headline: Tuesday is “Mars day”, a name that came from Chinese astrology in the Heian period.

sources.quote: /kaeubi/ → /kajoːbi/
Compound of 火曜 (kayō, “Mars (the planet)”, in reference also to the day for that planet, as originally imported from Chinese astrology in the Heian period) + 日 (hi, “day”).

The compound form suffixed with 日 (hi, “day”) appears in common use from the Meiji period with the promulgation of the Gregorian calendar. See also Names of the days of the week on Wikipedia.Wikipedia

headline: Wednesday is “Mercury day”, a name that came from Chinese astrology in the Heian period.

sources.quote: /suieubi/ > /suijoːbi/.
Compound of 水曜 (suiyō, “Mercury (the planet)”, in reference also to the day for that planet, as originally imported from Chinese astrology in the Heian period) + 日 (hi, “day”).

The compound form suffixed with 日 (hi, “day”) appears in common use from the Meiji period with the promulgation of the Gregorian calendar. See also Names of the days of the week on Wikipedia.Wikipedia

headline: Thursday is “Jupiter day”, a name that came from Chinese astrology in the Heian period.

sources.quote: /mokueubi/ > /mokujoːbi/.
Compound of 木曜 (mokuyō, “Jupiter (the planet)”, in reference also to the day for that planet, as originally imported from Chinese astrology in the Heian period) + 日 (hi, “day”).
The compound form suffixed with 日 (hi, “day”) appears in common use from the Meiji period with the promulgation of the Gregorian calendar.

headline: Friday is “Venus day”, a name that came from Chinese astrology in the Heian period.

sources.quote: /kiɴeubi/ → /kiɴjoːbi/
Compound of 金曜 (kin'yō, “Venus (the planet)”, in reference also to the day for that planet, as originally imported from Chinese astrology in the Heian period) + 日 (hi, “day”).

The compound form suffixed with 日 (hi, “day”) appears in common use from the Meiji period with the promulgation of the Gregorian calendar. See also Names of the days of the week on Wikipedia.Wikipedia

headline: Saturday is “Saturn day”, and its 日 voices to び.

sources.quote: /doeubi/ > /dojoːbi/

Compound of 土曜 (doyō, “Saturn (the planet)”, in reference also to the day for that planet, as originally imported from Chinese astrology in the Heian period) + 日 (hi, “day”). The hi changes to bi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

The compound form suffixed with 日 (hi, “day”) appears in common use from the Meiji period with the promulgation of the Gregorian calendar. See also Names of the days of the week on Wikipedia.Wikipedia

headline: Sunday is “Sun day”, and the -day compound first appears in 1826.

sources.quote: Compound of 日曜 (nichiyō, “Sun”, in reference also to the day for that celestial body, as originally imported from Chinese astrology in the Heian period) + 日 (hi, “day”).
The compound form suffixed with 日 (hi, “day”) first appears in 1826 and enters common use from the Meiji period with the promulgation of the Gregorian calendar.

headline: A well is a “water-well place” — and the 戸 in it may not be a door at all.

sources.quote: First attested in the Saibara.
Compound of 井 (i, “water well”) + 所 (to, “place”). The to changes to do as an instance of rendaku (連濁)..

headline: To swear an oath may once have meant to “mix blood”.

sources.quote: Probably originally a compound of 血 (chi, “blood”) + 交う (kau, “to cross, to blend, to mix”).

headline: A blackboard is a “black board” — and a native reading says the same with kuro and ita.

sources.quote: 黒 (koku, “black”) + 板 (ban, “board”)

headline: Twins are a “set of two” “children”, with こ voiced to ご.

sources.quote: 双(ふた) (futa, “set of two”) + 子(こ) (ko, “child”)
The ko changes to go as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Gas is an English word — but it also has a kanji spelling picked only for the sound.

sources.quote: From English gas. The kanji spelling is ateji.

headline: A son is a “begotten child” — and the 息 is a borrowed stand-in.

sources.quote: Compound of 生(む)す (musu, “to beget”) + 子(こ) (ko, “child”). 息 is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), from Middle Chinese 息子.

headline: “Cute” began as “embarrassing, shameful” — and the kanji have nothing to do with the sound.

sources.quote: /kawajui/ → /kawaiː/
Shift in pronunciation from kawayui below.

The kanji spelling 可愛い is an example of ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)), and uses an irregular reading of 愛. The phonological resemblance to Mandarin 可愛 (kě'ài), Min Nan 可愛 (khó-ài, “lovable”) is coincidental. Note that the medial -w- here is not an excrescence added between ka (可) and ai (愛), since the word is not formed from these morphemes.
Already realized phonetically as /kawaiː/ by the early 1600s, and possibly found alongside older form kawayui, as seen in the 1603 edition of the Nippo Jisho.

headline: Rōmaji has no “n” in it — the Roman part is Portuguese-derived ローマ with the Chinese-derived “character” 字.

sources.quote: ローマ (“Rome, Roman”) + 字 (“character”).
Note: There is no ン ("n") in ローマ字(じ) • (rōmaji) . ローマ is borrowed from Portuguese. Compare however ローマン体 (“roman type”), which uses ローマン; borrowed from English.

headline: The thumb is the “parent finger”.

sources.quote: Compound of 親 (oya, “parent, boss”) + 指 (yubi, “finger”).

meaning: part of word written in kana
headline: Okurigana are the kana “sent along afterward” — and the word is first attested in 1477.

sources.quote: Compound of 送(おく)り (okuri, “sending”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 送(おく)る (okuru, “to send”), from the sense of sending something afterward or adding something on the end) + 仮名(かな) (kana, “kana”). The kana changes to gana as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
First attested in 1477.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Oxygen is “sour element” — a calque of Dutch from the same 1834 book as hydrogen.

sources.quote: From 酸 (san, “acid”) + 素 (so, “element”), calque of Dutch zuurstof (literally “sourstuff”). Compare German Sauerstoff, Luxembourgish Sauerstoff, Indonesian zat asam. Coined by Japanese scientist Udagawa Yōan in 1834 in his book 遠西医方名物考補遺 (“酸素”).

headline: A cavity is a “bug tooth”, with は voiced to ば.

sources.quote: Compound of 虫 (mushi, “worm, bug”) + 歯 (ha, “tooth”). The ha changes to ba as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: The “wasei-eigo” motorcycle is, Wiktionary says, actually a real English word.

sources.quote: Clipping of オートバイシクル (ōtobaishikuru), erroneously listed in some monolingual Japanese dictionaries as wasei eigo, but actually borrowed from English autobicycle, an early English term for motorcycle. See also autobike.
First cited to a text from 1918.

headline: A baby is “red” plus an affectionate suffix, from the colour of a newborn's skin.

sources.quote: Compound of 赤 (aka, “red”) + ちゃん (-chan, familiarizing suffix).
Compare 赤ん坊 (akanbō) and 赤子 (akago), both of which also allude to the reddish complexion of a newborn. Compare also the similar formation of Malay anak merah (literally “child + red”).
First cited to a text from 1856 or 1857.

meaning: three days, third day of the month
headline: “Three days” grew out of an earlier “mika”, with a tensed sound added.

sources.quote: Tensening of earlier 三日 (mika); by surface analysis, 三 (mi, “three”) + 日 (-ka, “days”, counter for days).

headline: The toilet is the “place of convenience” — a coinage that Wiktionary dates to the late 1400s.

sources.quote: Appears to be a coinage in Japanese from Middle Chinese-derived roots, as a compound of 便 (ben, “convenience, ease”, also meaning “bodily waste; bowel movement”) + 所 (sho, “place”). The sho changes to jo as an instance of rendaku (連濁). Compare English expressions seat of ease, house of ease, also pooper, shitter.
First cited in works from the late 1400s.

headline: Kana means “borrowed name” — characters lent for their sounds.

sources.quote: /karina/ → /kanna/ → /kana/
Contraction of 仮(かん)名(な) (kanna) above. The reading may appear to be jūbakoyomi, but is instead actually an irregular development of the kun'yomi.

headline: A bar is a “drink place”, using an older form of the word for sake.

sources.quote: Compound of 酒(さか) (saka-, 被(ひ)覆(ふく)形(けい) (hifukukei, “bound form”) of 酒(さけ) (sake, “alcohol”)) + 場(ば) (ba, “place”).
